cat > /Users/mike/github/sw-ml-study/demo-decision-model/docs/plan.md <<'PLAN_EOF'
# Decision model delivery plan

## Outcome

Build a tiny, non-generative, typed decision model — a **TDM** — small enough
that every parameter, probability, and branch can be printed, and put it under
a microscope that shows the whole path from unstructured text to a typed
probabilistic decision to ordinary program logic to a canned string the model
never wrote.

The demonstration application is **Jeviza**: ELIZA with its 1966 pattern-matching
decision machinery replaced by a learned decision model, and with every word
ELIZA speaks still coming from a fixed, hand-written response table. The model
chooses; deterministic code speaks. The model can choose wrongly, but it cannot
invent an utterance that is not in the table. That property is the point of the
repository, and it is what makes "no hallucination" a structural claim here
rather than a marketing one.

The repository is the microscope; Jeviza is what is on the slide. A second
slide (campus navigation, in the manner of `../moe-microscope`'s docent) is
prepared but not required, to prove the mechanism is not ELIZA-shaped.

The headline question, which every experiment serves:

> Can a tiny non-generative model learn to replace ELIZA's hand-written
> decision rules while retaining deterministic, type-safe application behavior
> and useful **calibrated** uncertainty — and how small can it be?

That is a cleaner question than "can we clone Jev", and it is answerable with
measurements we can take ourselves.

## Naming and attribution

"System 1" is general cognitive-science vocabulary (Kahneman). **"System One
Model"** is TypeSafe's brand for their new model category, introduced with
**Jev**. TypeSafe has published Jev's *behavioral* contract — unstructured state
in, predefined typed outputs with probabilities, many questions answered in
parallel against one state, no autoregressive string generation, a two-stage
path for high-cardinality choices, and RLCD training aimed at calibration — but
not the architecture, the training algorithm, or weights.

Therefore:

- The thing we build is a **Typed Decision Model (TDM)**. We never call it a
  System One Model and never claim it reproduces Jev.
- Documentation says: *a small non-generative typed decision model inspired by
  the publicly described behavior of TypeSafe's Jev / System One Models.*
- Our calibration training stage is called **calibration fine-tuning**, never
  RLCD. We reproduce the stated *objective* (honest probabilities), not their
  undisclosed algorithm.
- Every claim about Jev in our documentation is quoted from the public post and
  marked as *their claim*, separate from *our measurement*.

The source discussion is retained verbatim at [`research.txt`](research.txt).

## What decides, and what the model may never do

This is the architecture rule, and it is load-bearing for the whole repository.

```text
        user text / conversation state
                      |
                      v
        +-----------------------------+
        |  TDM: state encoder + heads |   <-- the ONLY learned component
        +-----------------------------+
                      |
            typed probabilistic decision
            (Choice / Noul / Score)
                      |
                      v
        +-----------------------------+
        |  ordinary MLPL program       |  <-- thresholds, policy, retrieval,
        |  (policy, memory, templates) |      pronoun transforms, templates
        +-----------------------------+
                      |
                      v
              canned ELIZA string
```

The TDM's interface has exactly three primitives and no fourth:

| Primitive | Signature | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `choice` | `(state, question, choices[]) -> distribution` | probability per choice, selected id, confidence, margin |
| `noul`   | `(state, proposition) -> probability` | one probability in `[0,1]` |
| `score`  | `(state, levels[]) -> distribution + expectation` | distribution over an ordered scale, plus its expected value |

There is deliberately no:

```text
generate(prompt) -> String
```

Nothing in this repository may add one. Any string a user sees is a literal in
a committed response table, selected by index. A gate test asserts that every
emitted utterance is byte-identical to a table entry, so the property is
enforced by the build rather than by intention.

Thresholds, abstention, retrieval, escalation, and every side effect live in
MLPL code, never in the model. The model reports belief; the program decides
what to do about it.

## Builtin first, from scratch where it teaches

Prefer an existing sw-MLPL feature over an equivalent built here. Build a
mechanism from scratch only when watching it work is the lesson, and then show
both forms with a parity check between them. The catalog records each lesson as
`builtin`, `from-scratch`, or `both`.

| Mechanism | Builtin exists | Lesson form | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Embedding, linear, chain, ReLU, RMS norm, attention, softmax, sigmoid, cross-entropy, Adam, `train` | yes | builtin | no educational reason to rewrite them |
| Hashed word/bigram features, pooled text encoder | no builtin, but proven in `../moe-microscope/lib/docent.mlpl` | from-scratch, ported | the feature table is the student's whole input; it must be visible |
| Classic ELIZA keyword/rank/decomposition/reassembly engine | no | from-scratch | it is the oracle, the baseline, and half the lesson |
| Choice / Noul / Score primitives and the decision record | no | from-scratch | this is the subject of the repository |
| Binary cross-entropy | no builtin; `log`, `sigmoid`, `*`, `mean` are all differentiable | from-scratch, one line | needed for every Noul head |
| Temperature scaling | no | from-scratch | one scalar, fitted on validation; the cheapest calibration baseline |
| Platt scaling, isotonic regression (PAVA) | no | from-scratch | the calibration lesson *is* watching these run |
| Brier score, NLL, ECE, reliability bins, coverage curves | no | from-scratch | the measurements are the product |
| Top-k candidate selection | yes (`grade_down` stable argsort + `take`) | builtin | one line; do not rewrite argsort |
| Conversation memory store and retrieval | no | from-scratch | "state outside the model" is the lesson |
| Recording emission and playback | yes (`emit_frame`, `svg`, the Yew host in `../demo-extensions`) | builtin | dogfood the host, do not rebuild it |
| Decision instrument UI | no | from-scratch (Rust/Yew/WASM) | the instrument is a deliverable of equal standing to the model |

## Three questions answered up front

### 1. What exactly is the typed decision vocabulary?

Factored, never a cross-product. `RECALL_FAMILY_NEUTRAL_QUESTION` as one class
is the failure mode to avoid; it explodes combinatorially and gives every class
too few examples.

**Choice — `action` (10 classes, what ELIZA should do):**

| Action | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `GREET` | opening / greeting response |
| `YES` | response to affirmation |
| `NO` | response to negation |
| `DONT_KNOW` | response to expressed uncertainty |
| `REFLECT` | reflect the current statement back |
| `ASK_MORE` | ask the user to elaborate |
| `RECALL` | mention an earlier statement |
| `TOPIC_SHIFT` | move the conversation elsewhere |
| `KEYWORD` | classic keyword-driven response |
| `FALLBACK` | generic canned response |

**Choice — `topic` (16 classes, what it is about):**
`MOTHER`, `FATHER`, `FAMILY`, `SELF`, `FEELING`, `DESIRE`, `BELIEF`, `MEMORY`,
`DREAM`, `FEAR`, `WORK`, `POSSESSION`, `HEALTH`, `COMPUTER`, `SORRY`, `OTHER`.

**Noul — independent propositions (one sigmoid each):**
`mentions_family?`, `mentions_self?`, `contains_question?`, `negative_sentiment?`,
`short_answer?`, `memory_required?`, `repetitive?`, `mentions_computer?`.

**Score — ordered scales:**
`emotional_intensity` over `LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH`, reported both as a
distribution and as its expectation.

**Choice — `recall` (dynamic cardinality):** `{M1 … Mk, NONE}`, where the
candidates are supplied at call time by ordinary retrieval code and did not
exist at training time. This is the case that forces the question-conditioned
architecture (TD03) rather than a fixed head.

`OTHER`, `FALLBACK`, and `NONE` are first-class trained classes with deliberate
positive examples and hard negatives, not leftovers.

### 2. How do we teach the student, and what is allowed to define the truth?

A strict **label authority hierarchy**, highest first:

```text
1. the classic ELIZA rule engine   (exact, deterministic, free)
2. human-reviewed cases            (small, for disputes and the hard set)
3. teacher consensus               (>=2 of 3 teachers agree)
4. a single GPT teacher            (linguistic diversity only)
```

This matters: the GPT teacher is there to supply paraphrase, indirection, and
semantic generalization — **not** to define what ELIZA is. Without the hierarchy,
"distillation" quietly teaches the student to be a small modern chatbot instead
of ELIZA. Three data sources feed one corpus:

```text
        Classic ELIZA        templates          GPT teacher
        rules (oracle)       + mutation         conversations
              |                   |                   |
              +---------+---------+---------+---------+
                                  |
                        label-authority merge
                                  |
                        canonical soft labels
                                  |
                            train student
```

Teacher tiers, mirroring `../moe-microscope`'s arrangement so the lessons stay
runnable with no external dependency:

- **In-repo teacher (default, always runnable).** A deliberately larger MLPL
  TDM (wider embedding, attention encoder) trained on the rule-labeled corpus.
  Not strong, but measurably better than the student, fully inspectable, and
  offline.
- **External teacher (opt-in, gated).** A modest local quantized model through
  the gated native path documented in `../demo-ml-utils`, exporting the *same
  fixture schema* so no student code changes. The lesson records the teacher's
  identity, revision, and export budget, and exits with a documented status when
  the capability is unavailable.

Teachers emit **distributions, not labels** — `RECALL .55 / ASK_MORE .40 /
OTHER .05` is worth far more than `RECALL`. But a teacher's stated confidence is
never treated as a calibrated probability; that is precisely the property we
measure empirically and the weakness TypeSafe attributes to conventional LLMs.

The corpus is generated by **curriculum category**, so we always know what the
student is being asked to learn:

| Category | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `easy` | explicit keyword, classic ELIZA hit |
| `paraphrase` | semantic equivalent with the keyword removed |
| `ambiguous` | two genuinely plausible actions |
| `negative` | keyword present, wrong interpretation |
| `memory` | an earlier statement is worth recalling |
| `memory-negative` | nothing worth recalling; `NONE` is correct |
| `topic-shift` | conversation has gone repetitive |
| `short-input` | `yes` / `no` / `maybe` / `dunno` |
| `adversarial` | misleading keyword overlap |

Every accuracy number in the results table is reported **per category** as well
as overall. An overall 94% that is 99% on `easy` and 41% on `adversarial` is a
different result, and the table must say so.

### 3. What is the value demonstration?

A **pocket therapist** that runs from a file of a few hundred kilobytes, with no
generative model anywhere in the deployed path, and a side-by-side comparison
that isolates exactly what the learned component bought:

```text
                         INPUT
                           |
                  +--------+--------+
                  v                 v
            ELIZA 1966          Jeviza (TDM)
            keyword rules       learned decision
                  |                 |
            rule selection      probabilities + policy
                  |                 |
                  +--------+--------+
                           v
                  THE SAME RESPONSE TABLE
```

The headline comparison table, which the gate regenerates from a real run:

| Input | Classic selector | Learned selector |
|---|---|---|
| `my mother hates me` | `MOTHER` | `MOTHER` (high) |
| `mom never listens` | fallback | `MOTHER` (high) |
| `the woman who raised me worries` | fallback | `FAMILY` (moderate) |
| `I dreamed about mom` | `DREAM` | `DREAM` / `MOTHER` split |

And the **held-out lexicon experiment**, which is the cleanest single evidence
that the student learned meaning rather than keywords: hold `mom`, `mommy`,
`mama` entirely out of training; train on `mother`, `parent`, `family`; then
test `Mom won't leave me alone.` Classic ELIZA falls through. If the TDM says
`MOTHER` with well-calibrated confidence, the claim is demonstrated with a
number, not an anecdote.

## Evidence and current constraints

Measured against the adjacent `../sw-mlpl` checkout (`mlpl-repl 0.22.0`) and its
language reference. Nothing here is an upstream request yet.

**Confirmed available and sufficient:**

- Model DSL: `embed`, `linear`, `chain`, `relu_layer`, `rms_norm`,
  `causal_attention`, `softmax_layer`, `apply`, `predict_batch`, `param_count`,
  `param[shape]` leaves, reverse-mode `grad`, `adam`, `train N { }`,
  `experiment "name" { }`, `experiment_metric`.
- Decision math: `softmax(a, axis)`, `sigmoid`, `cross_entropy(logits, targets)`
  (fused, stable, differentiable), `one_hot`, `argmax(a, axis)`, `log`, `exp`,
  `mean`, `reduce(:add, a, axes)`.
- `gather_rows` is **differentiable** (backward is a scatter-add into addressed
  rows), so a from-scratch hashed feature table trains. This is the mechanism
  the whole student rests on.
- `grade_up` / `grade_down` are stable argsorts — exactly the top-k stage of the
  two-stage selector, with `gather_rows(C, grade_down(scores))` as the idiom.
- Text handling: `tokenize_bytes`, `train_bpe`, `str_len`, `str_slice`,
  `str_find`, `str_join`, `dedupe_rows`, `windows`.
- Observation: `emit_frame`, `svg` (`bar`, `line`, `scatter`, `heatmap`,
  `baseline`), `clock_ms`, `file_size`, `file_metadata`.
- Projection for the state-space diagram: `pca_components`, `mds`.

**Composed here, no builtin (each gets a lesson, not a complaint):**

- Binary cross-entropy for Noul heads — composed from `log`/`sigmoid`, all
  differentiable.
- Brier score, NLL, ECE, reliability bins, coverage-versus-accuracy curves.
- Temperature scaling, Platt scaling, isotonic regression (PAVA).
- Reliability diagram: composed from `scatter` + `line` + `baseline`; there is
  no `reliability` chart kind.

**To be probed in Saga 1, before anything depends on it:**

- `freeze` does not appear in the 0.22.0 language reference although it is
  referenced in peer plans. Probe `probes/p1_freeze_available.mlpl`; if absent,
  the frozen-encoder calibration lesson uses a stop-gradient idiom (recompute
  `h` outside `grad`) and the finding is filed.
- Gradient flow through a *two*-argument scorer `f(h_state, h_choice)` built
  from `matmul` + `concat` inside `grad`, which TD03 depends on.
- Whether `experiment` blocks compose with `train` inside a user function, which
  the sweep lessons depend on.

Every gap met gets a reproducer under `probes/`, a pinned mlplunit probe, a
workaround, and an entry in `docs/reference/sw-mlpl-findings.md`, in the same
step it is met.

## Architecture rule

```text
demo-decision-model (.mlpl model, ELIZA oracle, lessons, evaluation, calibration)
          |
          +-- decision instrument (Rust/Yew/WASM) ---> crates/ in THIS repo
          |
          +-- repeated domain-neutral helpers ------> ../demo-mlpl-libraries
          |
          +-- generic recording/playback need ------> ../demo-extensions
          |
          `-- proven language-wide blocker ---------> ../sw-mlpl
```

Sibling repositories are read-only from this project; work for them is written
down as a handoff in `docs/implementation/cross-repo-handoffs.md`, never
committed there from here.

The boundary inside this repo's Rust code: the instrument crates may know about
**decisions** — `Choice`, `Noul`, `Score`, distributions, confidence, thresholds,
the policy trace. They must not know about **ELIZA** — no `ElizaVisualizer`, no
hard-coded `MOTHER`, no response table in Rust. Class names, response strings,
and policy rules arrive as data in the trace. That is what lets the same
instrument render the campus-navigation slide without a line of new Rust, and
it is the test that the abstraction is real.

`sw-checklist` applies to the Rust crates.

## The TDM at two scales

The same MLPL source runs at two documented scales. The microscope scale is the
acceptance scale for every lesson.

| Component | Microscope scale (CPU, seconds) | Lab scale (opt-in, minutes) |
|---|---|---|
| Feature table | 512 hashed word + bigram slots | 4,096 slots or BPE vocabulary |
| Features per input | 24 padded (12 words + 11 bigrams) | 64 |
| `d_model` | 32 | 64 to 128 |
| Encoder | mean pool | pool / CNN / GRU / 1-head attention / SSM |
| Action head | 32 x 10 | 128 x 10 |
| Topic head | 32 x 16 | 128 x 16 |
| Noul heads | 8 x (32 x 1) | 8 x (128 x 1) |
| Score head | 32 x 3 | 128 x 3 |
| Scorer (TD03) | 32 x 32 bilinear + tiny MLP | 128 x 128 |
| Trainable parameters | roughly 17K to 60K | roughly 270K to 2M |
| Deployment form | INT8 packed file | same format |

The microscope-scale student is small enough to print in full. A 17K-parameter
model that handles ELIZA's decision surface is a *more* interesting result than
a 2M-parameter one, so the ladder starts at the floor and climbs only when a
measurement demands it. The research's illustrative ~274K figure (4K vocabulary
x 64 embedding) is the *upper* end of our starting range, not the target.

## The Decide → Gather → Decide → Act loop

This is the mechanism that lifts the project above "ELIZA with a classifier",
and it is what the instrument is built to show.

```text
                    USER TURN
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  Decision #1         |   choice(state, "what should ELIZA do?",
             |  What to do?         |          [GREET..FALLBACK])
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
                 RECALL = .84
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  ORDINARY CODE       |   cheap retrieval over the memory store:
             |  searches history    |   keyword overlap, topic tag, recency
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
              M1  M2  M3  M4  NONE      <-- candidates built at call time
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  Decision #2         |   choice(state, "which memory helps?",
             |  Which memory?       |          [M1..M4, NONE])
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
                    M3 = .62
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  ORDINARY CODE       |   pronoun transform + RECALL template
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
                        v
        "Earlier you said that work has been stressful.
         Tell me more about that."
```

The program, not the model, decides that more information is needed, gathers it,
and formulates the next typed question. The model never sees the whole
conversation, so conversation length does not grow model cost — the contrast
with stuffing a context window is measured, not asserted.

Conversation memory is a plain record, extracted deterministically:

```text
Memory {
  turn: 1,
  text: "My mother worries about me.",
  keywords: ["mother", "worries"],
  topic: FAMILY,
  age_turns: 11,
}
```

`NONE` is always in the candidate set. Forcing a classifier to pick the
least-wrong memory out of `{cereal, rain, printer, dog}` is the bug; a
well-trained `NONE .88` is the fix, and `if NONE > .60 { don't recall }` is
application policy sitting in MLPL where it can be read and changed.

## The decision instrument (Rust / Yew / WASM)

The instrument is a deliverable of equal standing to the model, developed from
the first lesson rather than after the last one. It must not look like a chat
window. It looks like a diagnostic instrument, and it shows, for every turn,
**the state that went in, the choices that were offered, and the typed decision
that came out** — plus the policy rule that consumed it.

```text
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
| JEVIZA -- typed decision microscope        turn 12/20   [<] [>] [||]  |
+----------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| STATE IN                   | DECISION OUT                            |
|                            |                                         |
| current utterance          | CHOICE  action        (10 offered)      |
|   "I don't know. Everything|   RECALL      ############   .61        |
|    just seems difficult."  |   REFLECT     ####           .18        |
|                            |   FALLBACK    ###            .12        |
| features (24 of 512 slots) |   ASK_MORE    ##             .09        |
|   [dont][know][everything] |   ...                                   |
|   [just][seems][difficult] |   confidence .61   margin .43           |
|   [dont know][know every.] |   calibrated: yes (T = 1.37)            |
|                            |                                         |
| memory store   11 turns    | NOUL                                    |
|   #2  FAMILY   age 10      |   memory_required?     .83              |
|   #5  WORK     age  7      |   short_answer?        .71              |
|   #8  HEALTH   age  4      |   contains_question?   .02              |
|   #9  WORK     age  3      |                                         |
|                            | SCORE  emotional_intensity              |
| CHOICES IN  (built by code)|   LOW .08  MED .57  HIGH .35  E = 1.27  |
|   M1 "my mother worries"   |                                         |
|   M2 "work has been..."    | CHOICE  recall        (5 offered)       |
|   M3 "I can't sleep"       |   M2          ###########    .48        |
|   M4 "my boss said..."     |   M3          ######         .27        |
|   NONE                     |   NONE        #              .05        |
+----------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| POLICY  memory_required > .60 AND max(recall) > .40  ->  RECALL_T03  |
| OUTPUT  (table entry 3, verbatim)                                    |
|   "Earlier you said that work has been stressful. Tell me more."     |
+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Three panes, always: **state in**, **choices in**, **decision out**, with the
policy rule and the verbatim table entry across the bottom. The user can step
turn by turn, and can open any single decision to see the distribution, the
confidence, the margin, whether calibration was applied, and which policy
branch consumed it.

Crates in this repository:

```text
crates/tdm-trace/        Decision-trace types, serde, schema validation. No UI.
crates/tdm-instrument/   Headless view model: panes, stepping, selection,
                         threshold overlays, reducer + transitions. No Yew.
crates/tdm-web/          Yew/WASM shell: renders the view model, nothing else.
schemas/decision-trace-v1.schema.json
```

Following the `mlpl-microscope-model` / `mlpl-microscope-web` split already
proven in `../demo-extensions`: the reducer and view model are headless and unit
tested in plain Rust; the Yew crate is a thin renderer. That is what keeps the
instrument testable without a browser.

MLPL lessons emit a `decision-trace-v1` document per run, pinned by hash under
`fixtures/traces/`, carrying a `provenance` block (producer, producer revision,
generation time, source description) in the manner of
`../demo-extensions/schemas/system-layout-v1.schema.json`. Each record is:

```json
{
  "turn": 12,
  "state": { "utterance": "...", "features": [...], "memory": [...] },
  "decisions": [
    { "kind": "choice", "question": "action", "labels": [...],
      "probs": [...], "selected": 6, "confidence": 0.61, "margin": 0.43,
      "calibration": { "method": "temperature", "t": 1.37 } },
    { "kind": "noul", "proposition": "memory_required?", "p": 0.83 },
    { "kind": "score", "scale": "emotional_intensity",
      "levels": ["LOW","MEDIUM","HIGH"], "probs": [...], "expectation": 1.27 }
  ],
  "policy": { "rule": "memory_required > .60 AND max(recall) > .40",
              "branch": "RECALL_T03" },
  "output": { "table": "recall", "index": 3, "text": "Earlier you said..." }
}
```

The page is a **playback**: no MLPL runs in the browser, and every number is
read from a pinned trace a real run wrote. A later saga adds the live path over
`mlpl-serve` SSE, reusing the mechanism proven in `../demo-extensions`.

An acceptance test asserts that `output.text` is byte-identical to the entry at
`output.index` of the committed response table. The instrument cannot show a
string the table does not contain, and neither can Jeviza.

## Visual and measurement contract

Applies to every lesson in every saga.

**Every data structure and transformation gets a diagram.** The feature table,
the pooled state, each head's logits, the distribution, the memory store, the
candidate set, the calibration map, the policy branch — each drawn once with
shape, dtype, byte size, and axis meanings; each transformation drawn as
before -> operation -> after with the fixture's exact values on the arrows.
Diagrams are generated from the same recorded values the tests assert on. Static
SVG under `assets/previews/` is the canonical committed form. Color is never the
only carrier of meaning; every diagram has a title, a description, and a numeric
table beside it.

**Every lesson measures three axes** and records them in its catalog entry:

| Axis | Required measurements | How |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | trainable parameters, active parameters per decision, feature-table bytes, packed-file bytes, memory-store bytes, trace bytes | `param_count`, explicit shape arithmetic, `file_size` |
| Speed | decisions per forward pass, encoder evaluations per turn, candidates scored per turn, and wall-clock microseconds per decision and milliseconds per training step | counted costs are the deterministic primary metric; `clock_ms()` is the machine-dependent secondary, reported with the binary version |
| Quality | per-head accuracy (action, topic, noul, score, recall), top-2 accuracy, per-category accuracy, NLL, Brier, ECE, reliability bins, coverage at target accuracy, teacher/student KL, abstention rate | the evaluation harness over the fixed split, with the rule engine as oracle |

**Accuracy alone is not a result.** Every quality claim reports the
accuracy-versus-coverage curve, because the number the application actually
needs is "at what threshold can code act autonomously, and how much of the
traffic does that cover":

| Threshold | Answered automatically | Accuracy when answered |
|---|---|---|
| 0.50 | ... | ... |
| 0.60 | ... | ... |
| 0.70 | ... | ... |
| 0.80 | ... | ... |
| 0.90 | ... | ... |

Every run appends one row to `docs/reference/results.md`, keyed by lesson ID,
configuration, and binary version, so the comparison matrix fills in as sagas
complete rather than being promised.

## Experimental progression

| Stage | Lesson | Mechanism | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `EZ01` | classic ELIZA engine in MLPL (keywords, ranks, decomposition, reassembly) | the symbolic baseline and the labeling oracle |
| 0a | `EZ02` | the response table and deterministic transforms, isolated | what is the bounded output space, exactly? |
| 1 | `DS01` | rule + template corpus generator with curriculum categories | can we make labels cheaply and know what they teach? |
| 2 | `TD01` | fixed-class student: hashed features -> pool -> one action head | can a tiny model replace keyword rules at all? |
| 3 | `TD02` | factored multi-head: action, topic, 8 nouls, score — one pass | many typed decisions from one state representation |
| 4 | `TD03` | question-conditioned scorer `f(h_state, h_question, h_choice)` | can choices be *inputs*, so unseen candidates can be scored? |
| 5 | `CB01` | reliability, ECE, Brier, NLL; temperature / Platt / isotonic | does `.80` actually mean 80%? |
| 6 | `CB02` | calibration fine-tuning (`L_CE + lambda L_Brier`) | does training for calibration beat fixing it afterwards? |
| 7 | `AB01` | `OTHER` / `NONE` training and coverage curves | what does abstention buy, and at what threshold? |
| 8 | `MM01` | structured memory store and deterministic retrieval | state outside the model |
| 9 | `MM02` | the `RECALL` decision and the Decide -> Gather -> Decide loop | the model requests an operation; code performs it |
| 10 | `TS01` | independent scoring -> `grade_down` top-k -> comparative choice | the high-cardinality two-stage path |
| 11 | `TE01` | in-repo teacher exporting soft targets | a runnable teacher with no external dependency |
| 12 | `TE02` | external GPT teacher (gated), same fixture schema | linguistic diversity and indirection |
| 13 | `TE03` | teacher ensemble, disagreement as a signal | does consensus improve corpus quality? |
| 14 | `KD01` | soft-label distillation, `KL(teacher \|\| student)` vs `CE` | is the teacher's uncertainty worth keeping? |
| 15 | `AD01` | active distillation: student uncertainty selects what to label | how far does teacher cost fall? |
| 16 | `EN01` | encoder ladder: bag-of-words -> pool -> CNN -> GRU -> attention -> SSM | how much encoder does this decision surface need? |
| 17 | `MX01` | MoE encoder | is conditional compute worth it at this scale? |
| 18 | `RB01` | resource budget: INT8/INT4, packed file, microseconds per decision | what does the deployed artifact actually cost? |
| 19 | `MB01` | keyword-matcher yardstick, held-out-lexicon split | did the learned component actually buy anything? |

`MB01` is deliberately last in the table and first in spirit: `../moe-microscope`
recorded a docent that did not beat a deterministic matcher, and that honesty is
the standard here. Every learned lesson reports its margin over the matcher on
the same split, and a negative margin is published as a result.

## Visualization track, every saga

The instrument is dogfooded from Saga 1, not built at the end.

- Every lesson emits a `decision-trace-v1` document, pinned by hash under
  `fixtures/traces/`.
- Every saga ends with an instrument step: the new traces render in the Yew host
  with no lesson-specific Rust added, and any schema or budget gap is reported
  the way language findings are.
- Committed SVG diagrams remain the canonical README evidence; the instrument
  adds stepping and selection, never a second implementation of a lesson.
- The live (`mlpl-serve` SSE) path starts once three traces exist.

## Saga 1: foundation, probes, the ELIZA oracle, and the response table

1. **foundation-contract.** `agentrail setup`; `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
   `justfile`, `mlplunit.conf`, `scripts/`, `catalog/lessons.toml`, the docs
   skeleton, `COPYRIGHT`, `LICENSE`, and the README.
2. **language-probes.** The three Saga-1 probes above (`freeze`, two-argument
   scorer gradients, `experiment` inside a user function), each with a pinned
   mlplunit probe and a findings entry.
3. **eliza-engine (EZ01).** The classic engine in MLPL: keyword list with ranks,
   decomposition patterns, reassembly rules, the pronoun transform, and the
   memory stack ELIZA itself had. Tests pin its output on a fixed transcript so
   it is a *deterministic oracle*, not an approximation of one.
4. **response-table (EZ02).** The response table as committed data, with the
   byte-identity gate test and the diagram of the bounded output space.
5. **matcher-yardstick (MB01).** The keyword matcher scored on the evaluation
   split, with the held-out-lexicon split defined here so no later lesson can
   quietly choose an easier one.

Exit: a deterministic ELIZA runs, its output space is enumerated and gated, the
yardstick has a published number, and the probes have answers.

## Saga 2: the corpus and the first student

1. **corpus-generator (DS01).** Template and mutation generator producing all
   nine curriculum categories, with the oracle labeling everything it can. The
   split is fixed here and never regenerated.
2. **first-student (TD01).** Hashed word+bigram features (porting the technique
   from `../moe-microscope/lib/docent.mlpl`), mean pool, one action head,
   `cross_entropy`, `adam`. Parameter count printed in full.
3. **first-trace.** The `decision-trace-v1` schema, the first pinned trace, and
   the first instrument render.
4. **student-vs-matcher.** TD01 against MB01 on the same split, per category.

Exit: a learned selector exists, its margin over the matcher is published per
category, and one trace renders in the instrument.

## Saga 3: typed primitives and question-conditioned decisions

1. **factored-heads (TD02).** Action, topic, eight Nouls, and the score scale
   from one shared encoder in one forward pass. Per-head losses summed;
   binary cross-entropy composed for the Nouls. The "one pass, many decisions"
   diagram is drawn from real recorded values.
2. **decision-record.** The `choice` / `noul` / `score` MLPL contract, with the
   confidence and margin definitions fixed once and reused everywhere.
3. **question-conditioned-scorer (TD03).** `score_i = f(h_state, h_question,
   h_choice_i)`, trained over `(state, question, choices, answer)` tuples so the
   same model answers questions whose choices it never saw. Compared head to
   head with the fixed-head TD02 on the questions both can answer — the cost of
   generality, measured.
4. **cross-encoder-comparison.** The accurate-but-repeated cross-encoder against
   the shared-state encoder, on accuracy and on encoder evaluations per turn.

Exit: three primitives implemented, the general form works, and the generality
cost is a number.

## Saga 4: calibration and abstention

1. **calibration-measurement (CB01).** Reliability bins, ECE, Brier, NLL,
   and the reliability diagram composed from `scatter` + `line` + `baseline`.
2. **post-hoc-calibration.** Temperature scaling, Platt scaling, and isotonic
   regression (PAVA) from scratch, fitted on validation, compared on the same
   table: accuracy, ECE, Brier before and after.
3. **calibration-training (CB02).** `L = L_CE + lambda L_Brier`, swept over
   lambda, against the post-hoc baselines. The honest question this saga exists
   to answer: *at this scale, is anything beyond temperature scaling necessary?*
   A "no" is a publishable result.
4. **abstention (AB01).** `OTHER` / `NONE` with deliberate positives and hard
   negatives; the coverage-versus-accuracy table; the policy idiom
   `if confidence >= t { act } else { fallback }` shown in MLPL.
5. **instrument-calibration.** The instrument shows whether a distribution is
   raw or calibrated, and by what map.

Exit: the reliability diagram, the three-way calibration comparison, and the
coverage table are all in the results file and rendered in the instrument.

## Saga 5: conversation memory and two-stage selection

1. **memory-store (MM01).** The structured memory record, deterministic
   extraction, and the cheap retriever (keyword overlap, topic tag, recency)
   with its own accuracy number — retrieval quality measured separately from
   decision quality, because conflating them is how this gets misread.
2. **recall-decision (MM02).** The full Decide -> Gather -> Decide -> Act loop,
   with `NONE` in every candidate set and the `memory-negative` category
   carrying real weight.
3. **two-stage-selector (TS01).** Independent sigmoid scoring of up to 100
   memories, `grade_down` top-k, then a comparative softmax over the survivors;
   compared against single-stage selection over the same candidates on accuracy
   and on candidates scored per turn. This is the mechanism TypeSafe describes
   for high-cardinality choices, and we arrived at it independently for this
   problem — worth saying plainly in the write-up.
4. **memory-instrument.** The instrument's memory pane: store, retrieved
   candidates, the second decision, and the `NONE` threshold.

Exit: "Earlier you said..." works without a context window, and the cost of
conversation length is measured rather than assumed.

## Saga 6: teachers, distillation, and active labeling

1. **in-repo-teacher (TE01).** The larger MLPL TDM and its soft-target fixture
   schema.
2. **external-teacher (TE02).** The gated local-model path, same schema,
   recorded identity/revision/budget, documented skip status when unavailable.
3. **teacher-ensemble (TE03).** Three teachers, agreement as a weight,
   disagreement routed to the hard set. Dataset quality measured as downstream
   student accuracy, not as a self-reported score.
4. **distillation (KD01).** `KL(teacher || student)` against plain `CE`, and the
   mixed objective, with the label-authority hierarchy enforced in code so the
   rule engine always outranks a teacher.
5. **active-distillation (AD01).** Cheap student triage: confident examples skip
   the teacher, uncertain ones are labeled. Report teacher calls saved at equal
   student accuracy — the number that makes this worth doing.

Exit: the distillation pipeline runs end to end offline, and teacher cost per
point of student accuracy is a published curve.

## Saga 7: the encoder frontier and the deployed artifact

1. **encoder-ladder (EN01).** Bag-of-words logistic regression, mean pool, MLP,
   CNN, GRU, 1-head attention, and a state-space block — same corpus, same
   heads, same split. Plotted as accuracy and ECE against parameters and
   microseconds per decision, so the knee of the curve is visible.
2. **moe-encoder (MX01).** A routed encoder, connecting directly to
   `../moe-microscope`'s conditional-compute work.
3. **resource-budget (RB01).** INT8 then INT4 weights, the packed file, bytes
   and microseconds per decision, and the quality lost at each step.
4. **pocket-therapist.** The deployed artifact: the packed file plus the response
   table, running the whole loop with no generative model present.

Exit: the smallest configuration that meets a stated accuracy-and-calibration
bar is identified by measurement, and it ships as a file.

## Saga 8: the instrument, complete

1. **instrument-complete.** Every decision kind, stepping, selection, threshold
   overlays, the policy trace, and the side-by-side classic/learned comparison
   mode in one page.
2. **ambiguity-theatre.** The deliberately ambiguous inputs — `I dreamed my
   mother was a computer.` — with the policy panel editable, so a viewer can
   watch `if confidence < .50 -> DEFAULT` and `if dream > .30 -> DREAM` produce
   different behavior from *identical* model output. Prediction and policy,

3. **live-path.** The `mlpl-serve` SSE path: edit the lesson, rerun, watch the

4. **second-slide.** A campus-navigation trace rendered by the same instrument

works, and a non-ELIZA trace renders unmodified.

## Saga 9: findings and recommendations

The report: what a tiny typed decision model can and cannot do; where
calibration training paid and where temperature scaling was enough; what the
learned selector bought over keyword matching, per category, with the
held-out-lexicon result stated plainly; the teacher-cost curve; the parameter /
latency / accuracy / ECE frontier; and an explicit list of what we could *not*
determine about Jev from public information, so the boundary between our
measurements and their claims stays legible.

## Cross-cutting gates

- Every executable behavior starts with native mlplunit coverage; `just check`
  is the full pre-commit gate and grows with each lesson's demo and fixture
  freshness checks.
- Every `.mlpl` file has a module-purpose comment, every user function has a
  first-expression docstring, and canonical formatting is checked before commit
  and push with `scripts/check-mlpl-style`.
- **The no-generation gate.** A test asserts that every string Jeviza can emit
  is byte-identical to a committed response-table entry, reached by index. This
  runs on every commit. It is the repository's central claim, so it is enforced
  mechanically.
- Every lesson satisfies the visual and measurement contract and adds a catalog
  entry naming its source, tests, previews, trace, fixture, triple, and
  implementation form.
- Every quality claim carries its per-category breakdown, its calibration
  numbers, and its margin over the `MB01` matcher on the same split.
- Every language or host gap gets a reproducer under `probes/`, a pinned
  mlplunit probe, a workaround, and a findings entry, in the same step it is met.
- Lessons are deterministic, bounded, standalone, and honest about which work
  runs in MLPL, in a builtin, in Rust, or in a simulator.
- Sibling repositories remain read-only; their work is written as a handoff.
- `sw-checklist` applies to the Rust crates.

## Non-goals

- A better chatbot. Response quality is fixed by a 1966 table and is not an
  objective; only *selection* quality is measured.
- Any generative path at inference. No decoder, no sampling into text, no
  string the response table does not contain.
- Reproducing Jev, its architecture, or RLCD. We reproduce the published
  *behavioral contract* and the *objective*, and say so every time.
- Claiming schema conformance implies correctness. A typed output cannot be
  outside the permitted space; it can still be the wrong choice, and the
  coverage tables exist to say how often.
- Treating a teacher's stated confidence as a calibrated probability.
- ELIZA-specific types in the Rust instrument crates.
- Training on a microcontroller; the MCU/NPU/FPGA track is an inference target

# Decision model delivery plan

## Outcome

Build a tiny, non-generative, typed decision model — a **TDM** — small enough
that every parameter, probability, and branch can be printed, and put it under
a microscope that shows the whole path from unstructured text to a typed
probabilistic decision to ordinary program logic to a canned string the model
never wrote.

The demonstration application is **Jeviza**: ELIZA with its 1966 pattern-matching
decision machinery replaced by a learned decision model, and with every word
ELIZA speaks still coming from a fixed, hand-written response table. The model
chooses; deterministic code speaks. The model can choose wrongly, but it cannot
invent an utterance that is not in the table. That property is the point of the
repository, and it is what makes "no hallucination" a structural claim here
rather than a marketing one.

The repository is the microscope; Jeviza is what is on the slide. A second
slide (campus navigation, in the manner of `../moe-microscope`'s docent) is
prepared but not required, to prove the mechanism is not ELIZA-shaped.

The headline question, which every experiment serves:

> Can a tiny non-generative model learn to replace ELIZA's hand-written
> decision rules while retaining deterministic, type-safe application behavior
> and useful **calibrated** uncertainty — and how small can it be?

That is a cleaner question than "can we clone Jev", and it is answerable with
measurements we can take ourselves.

## Naming and attribution

"System 1" is general cognitive-science vocabulary (Kahneman). **"System One
Model"** is TypeSafe's brand for their new model category, introduced with
**Jev**. TypeSafe has published Jev's *behavioral* contract — unstructured state
in, predefined typed outputs with probabilities, many questions answered in
parallel against one state, no autoregressive string generation, a two-stage
path for high-cardinality choices, and RLCD training aimed at calibration — but
not the architecture, the training algorithm, or weights.

Therefore:

- The thing we build is a **Typed Decision Model (TDM)**. We never call it a
  System One Model and never claim it reproduces Jev.
- Documentation says: *a small non-generative typed decision model inspired by
  the publicly described behavior of TypeSafe's Jev / System One Models.*
- Our calibration training stage is called **calibration fine-tuning**, never
  RLCD. We reproduce the stated *objective* (honest probabilities), not their
  undisclosed algorithm.
- Every claim about Jev in our documentation is quoted from the public post and
  marked as *their claim*, separate from *our measurement*.

The source discussion is retained verbatim at [`research.txt`](research.txt).

## What decides, and what the model may never do

This is the architecture rule, and it is load-bearing for the whole repository.

```text
        user text / conversation state
                      |
                      v
        +-----------------------------+
        |  TDM: state encoder + heads |   <-- the ONLY learned component
        +-----------------------------+
                      |
            typed probabilistic decision
            (Choice / Noul / Score)
                      |
                      v
        +-----------------------------+
        |  ordinary MLPL program       |  <-- thresholds, policy, retrieval,
        |  (policy, memory, templates) |      pronoun transforms, templates
        +-----------------------------+
                      |
                      v
              canned ELIZA string
```

The TDM's interface has exactly three primitives and no fourth:

| Primitive | Signature | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `choice` | `(state, question, choices[]) -> distribution` | probability per choice, selected id, confidence, margin |
| `noul`   | `(state, proposition) -> probability` | one probability in `[0,1]` |
| `score`  | `(state, levels[]) -> distribution + expectation` | distribution over an ordered scale, plus its expected value |

There is deliberately no:

```text
generate(prompt) -> String
```

Nothing in this repository may add one. Any string a user sees is a literal in
a committed response table, selected by index. A gate test asserts that every
emitted utterance is byte-identical to a table entry, so the property is
enforced by the build rather than by intention.

Thresholds, abstention, retrieval, escalation, and every side effect live in
MLPL code, never in the model. The model reports belief; the program decides
what to do about it.

## Builtin first, from scratch where it teaches

Prefer an existing sw-MLPL feature over an equivalent built here. Build a
mechanism from scratch only when watching it work is the lesson, and then show
both forms with a parity check between them. The catalog records each lesson as
`builtin`, `from-scratch`, or `both`.

| Mechanism | Builtin exists | Lesson form | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Embedding, linear, chain, ReLU, RMS norm, attention, softmax, sigmoid, cross-entropy, Adam, `train` | yes | builtin | no educational reason to rewrite them |
| Hashed word/bigram features, pooled text encoder | no builtin, but proven in `../moe-microscope/lib/docent.mlpl` | from-scratch, ported | the feature table is the student's whole input; it must be visible |
| Classic ELIZA keyword/rank/decomposition/reassembly engine | no | from-scratch | it is the oracle, the baseline, and half the lesson |
| Choice / Noul / Score primitives and the decision record | no | from-scratch | this is the subject of the repository |
| Binary cross-entropy | no builtin; `log`, `sigmoid`, `*`, `mean` are all differentiable | from-scratch, one line | needed for every Noul head |
| Temperature scaling | no | from-scratch | one scalar, fitted on validation; the cheapest calibration baseline |
| Platt scaling, isotonic regression (PAVA) | no | from-scratch | the calibration lesson *is* watching these run |
| Brier score, NLL, ECE, reliability bins, coverage curves | no | from-scratch | the measurements are the product |
| Top-k candidate selection | yes (`grade_down` stable argsort + `take`) | builtin | one line; do not rewrite argsort |
| Conversation memory store and retrieval | no | from-scratch | "state outside the model" is the lesson |
| Recording emission and playback | yes (`emit_frame`, `svg`, the Yew host in `../demo-extensions`) | builtin | dogfood the host, do not rebuild it |
| Decision instrument UI | no | from-scratch (Rust/Yew/WASM) | the instrument is a deliverable of equal standing to the model |

## Three questions answered up front

### 1. What exactly is the typed decision vocabulary?

Factored, never a cross-product. `RECALL_FAMILY_NEUTRAL_QUESTION` as one class
is the failure mode to avoid; it explodes combinatorially and gives every class
too few examples.

**Choice — `action` (10 classes, what ELIZA should do):**

| Action | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `GREET` | opening / greeting response |
| `YES` | response to affirmation |
| `NO` | response to negation |
| `DONT_KNOW` | response to expressed uncertainty |
| `REFLECT` | reflect the current statement back |
| `ASK_MORE` | ask the user to elaborate |
| `RECALL` | mention an earlier statement |
| `TOPIC_SHIFT` | move the conversation elsewhere |
| `KEYWORD` | classic keyword-driven response |
| `FALLBACK` | generic canned response |

**Choice — `topic` (16 classes, what it is about):**
`MOTHER`, `FATHER`, `FAMILY`, `SELF`, `FEELING`, `DESIRE`, `BELIEF`, `MEMORY`,
`DREAM`, `FEAR`, `WORK`, `POSSESSION`, `HEALTH`, `COMPUTER`, `SORRY`, `OTHER`.

**Noul — independent propositions (one sigmoid each):**
`mentions_family?`, `mentions_self?`, `contains_question?`, `negative_sentiment?`,
`short_answer?`, `memory_required?`, `repetitive?`, `mentions_computer?`.

**Score — ordered scales:**
`emotional_intensity` over `LOW | MEDIUM | HIGH`, reported both as a
distribution and as its expectation.

**Choice — `recall` (dynamic cardinality):** `{M1 … Mk, NONE}`, where the
candidates are supplied at call time by ordinary retrieval code and did not
exist at training time. This is the case that forces the question-conditioned
architecture (TD03) rather than a fixed head.

`OTHER`, `FALLBACK`, and `NONE` are first-class trained classes with deliberate
positive examples and hard negatives, not leftovers.

### 2. How do we teach the student, and what is allowed to define the truth?

A strict **label authority hierarchy**, highest first:

```text
1. the classic ELIZA rule engine   (exact, deterministic, free)
2. human-reviewed cases            (small, for disputes and the hard set)
3. teacher consensus               (>=2 of 3 teachers agree)
4. a single GPT teacher            (linguistic diversity only)
```

This matters: the GPT teacher is there to supply paraphrase, indirection, and
semantic generalization — **not** to define what ELIZA is. Without the hierarchy,
"distillation" quietly teaches the student to be a small modern chatbot instead
of ELIZA. Three data sources feed one corpus:

```text
        Classic ELIZA        templates          GPT teacher
        rules (oracle)       + mutation         conversations
              |                   |                   |
              +---------+---------+---------+---------+
                                  |
                        label-authority merge
                                  |
                        canonical soft labels
                                  |
                            train student
```

Teacher tiers, mirroring `../moe-microscope`'s arrangement so the lessons stay
runnable with no external dependency:

- **In-repo teacher (default, always runnable).** A deliberately larger MLPL
  TDM (wider embedding, attention encoder) trained on the rule-labeled corpus.
  Not strong, but measurably better than the student, fully inspectable, and
  offline.
- **External teacher (opt-in, gated).** A modest local quantized model through
  the gated native path documented in `../demo-ml-utils`, exporting the *same
  fixture schema* so no student code changes. The lesson records the teacher's
  identity, revision, and export budget, and exits with a documented status when
  the capability is unavailable.

Teachers emit **distributions, not labels** — `RECALL .55 / ASK_MORE .40 /
OTHER .05` is worth far more than `RECALL`. But a teacher's stated confidence is
never treated as a calibrated probability; that is precisely the property we
measure empirically and the weakness TypeSafe attributes to conventional LLMs.

The corpus is generated by **curriculum category**, so we always know what the
student is being asked to learn:

| Category | What it contains |
|---|---|
| `easy` | explicit keyword, classic ELIZA hit |
| `paraphrase` | semantic equivalent with the keyword removed |
| `ambiguous` | two genuinely plausible actions |
| `negative` | keyword present, wrong interpretation |
| `memory` | an earlier statement is worth recalling |
| `memory-negative` | nothing worth recalling; `NONE` is correct |
| `topic-shift` | conversation has gone repetitive |
| `short-input` | `yes` / `no` / `maybe` / `dunno` |
| `adversarial` | misleading keyword overlap |

Every accuracy number in the results table is reported **per category** as well
as overall. An overall 94% that is 99% on `easy` and 41% on `adversarial` is a
different result, and the table must say so.

### 3. What is the value demonstration?

A **pocket therapist** that runs from a file of a few hundred kilobytes, with no
generative model anywhere in the deployed path, and a side-by-side comparison
that isolates exactly what the learned component bought:

```text
                         INPUT
                           |
                  +--------+--------+
                  v                 v
            ELIZA 1966          Jeviza (TDM)
            keyword rules       learned decision
                  |                 |
            rule selection      probabilities + policy
                  |                 |
                  +--------+--------+
                           v
                  THE SAME RESPONSE TABLE
```

The headline comparison table, which the gate regenerates from a real run:

| Input | Classic selector | Learned selector |
|---|---|---|
| `my mother hates me` | `MOTHER` | `MOTHER` (high) |
| `mom never listens` | fallback | `MOTHER` (high) |
| `the woman who raised me worries` | fallback | `FAMILY` (moderate) |
| `I dreamed about mom` | `DREAM` | `DREAM` / `MOTHER` split |

And the **held-out lexicon experiment**, which is the cleanest single evidence
that the student learned meaning rather than keywords: hold `mom`, `mommy`,
`mama` entirely out of training; train on `mother`, `parent`, `family`; then
test `Mom won't leave me alone.` Classic ELIZA falls through. If the TDM says
`MOTHER` with well-calibrated confidence, the claim is demonstrated with a
number, not an anecdote.

## The TDM at two scales

The same MLPL source runs at two documented scales. The microscope scale is the
acceptance scale for every lesson.

| Component | Microscope scale (CPU, seconds) | Lab scale (opt-in, minutes) |
|---|---|---|
| Feature table | 512 hashed word + bigram slots | 4,096 slots or BPE vocabulary |
| Features per input | 24 padded (12 words + 11 bigrams) | 64 |
| `d_model` | 32 | 64 to 128 |
| Encoder | mean pool | pool / CNN / GRU / 1-head attention / SSM |
| Action head | 32 x 10 | 128 x 10 |
| Topic head | 32 x 16 | 128 x 16 |
| Noul heads | 8 x (32 x 1) | 8 x (128 x 1) |
| Score head | 32 x 3 | 128 x 3 |
| Scorer (TD03) | 32 x 32 bilinear + tiny MLP | 128 x 128 |
| Trainable parameters | roughly 17K to 60K | roughly 270K to 2M |
| Deployment form | INT8 packed file | same format |

The microscope-scale student is small enough to print in full. A 17K-parameter
model that handles ELIZA's decision surface is a *more* interesting result than
a 2M-parameter one, so the ladder starts at the floor and climbs only when a
measurement demands it. The research's illustrative ~274K figure (4K vocabulary
x 64 embedding) is the *upper* end of our starting range, not the target.

## The Decide → Gather → Decide → Act loop

This is the mechanism that lifts the project above "ELIZA with a classifier",
and it is what the instrument is built to show.

```text
                    USER TURN
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  Decision #1         |   choice(state, "what should ELIZA do?",
             |  What to do?         |          [GREET..FALLBACK])
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
                 RECALL = .84
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  ORDINARY CODE       |   cheap retrieval over the memory store:
             |  searches history    |   keyword overlap, topic tag, recency
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
              M1  M2  M3  M4  NONE      <-- candidates built at call time
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  Decision #2         |   choice(state, "which memory helps?",
             |  Which memory?       |          [M1..M4, NONE])
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
                    M3 = .62
                        |
                        v
             +----------------------+
             |  ORDINARY CODE       |   pronoun transform + RECALL template
             +----------+-----------+
                        |
                        v
        "Earlier you said that work has been stressful.
         Tell me more about that."
```

The program, not the model, decides that more information is needed, gathers it,
and formulates the next typed question. The model never sees the whole
conversation, so conversation length does not grow model cost — the contrast
with stuffing a context window is measured, not asserted.

Conversation memory is a plain record, extracted deterministically:

```text
Memory {
  turn: 1,
  text: "My mother worries about me.",
  keywords: ["mother", "worries"],
  topic: FAMILY,
  age_turns: 11,
}
```

`NONE` is always in the candidate set. Forcing a classifier to pick the
least-wrong memory out of `{cereal, rain, printer, dog}` is the bug; a
well-trained `NONE .88` is the fix, and `if NONE > .60 { don't recall }` is
application policy sitting in MLPL where it can be read and changed.

## The decision instrument (Rust / Yew / WASM)

The instrument is a deliverable of equal standing to the model, developed from
the first lesson rather than after the last one. It must not look like a chat
window. It looks like a diagnostic instrument, and it shows, for every turn,
**the state that went in, the choices that were offered, and the typed decision
that came out** — plus the policy rule that consumed it.

```text

|                            |                                         |

|    just seems difficult."  |   REFLECT     ####           .18        |
|                            |   FALLBACK    ###            .12        |
| features (24 of 512 slots) |   ASK_MORE    ##             .09        |
|   [dont][know][everything] |   ...                                   |
|   [just][seems][difficult] |   confidence .61   margin .43           |
|   [dont know][know every.] |   calibrated: yes (T = 1.37)            |
|                            |                                         |
| memory store   11 turns    | NOUL                                    |
|   #2  FAMILY   age 10      |   memory_required?     .83              |
|   #5  WORK     age  7      |   short_answer?        .71              |
|   #8  HEALTH   age  4      |   contains_question?   .02              |
|   #9  WORK     age  3      |                                         |
|                            | SCORE  emotional_intensity              |
| CHOICES IN  (built by code)|   LOW .08  MED .57  HIGH .35  E = 1.27  |
|   M1 "my mother worries"   |                                         |
|   M2 "work has been..."    | CHOICE  recall        (5 offered)       |
|   M3 "I can't sleep"       |   M2          ###########    .48        |
|   M4 "my boss said..."     |   M3          ######         .27        |
|   NONE                     |   NONE        #              .05        |
+----------------------------+-----------------------------------------+
| POLICY  memory_required > .60 AND max(recall) > .40  ->  RECALL_T03  |

+----------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Three panes, always: **state in**, **choices in**, **decision out**, with the
policy rule and the verbatim table entry across the bottom. The user can step
turn by turn, and can open any single decision to see the distribution, the
confidence, the margin, whether calibration was applied, and which policy
branch consumed it.

{

  "state": { "utterance": "...", "features": [...], "memory": [...] },
  "decisions": [
    { "kind": "choice", "question": "action", "labels": [...],
      "probs": [...], "selected": 6, "confidence": 0.61, "margin": 0.43,
      "calibration": { "method": "temperature", "t": 1.37 } },
    { "kind": "noul", "proposition": "memory_required?", "p": 0.83 },
    { "kind": "score", "scale": "emotional_intensity",
      "levels": ["LOW","MEDIUM","HIGH"], "probs": [...], "expectation": 1.27 }
  ],
  "policy": { "rule": "memory_required > .60 AND max(recall) > .40",
              "branch": "RECALL_T03" },
  "output": { "table": "recall", "index": 3, "text": "Earlier you said..." }
}
```

The page is a **playback**: no MLPL runs in the browser, and every number is
read from a pinned trace a real run wrote. A later saga adds the live path over
`mlpl-serve` SSE, reusing the mechanism proven in `../demo-extensions`.

An acceptance test asserts that `output.text` is byte-identical to the entry at
`output.index` of the committed response table. The instrument cannot show a
string the table does not contain, and neither can Jeviza.

## Visual and measurement contract

Applies to every lesson in every saga.

**Every data structure and transformation gets a diagram.** The feature table,
the pooled state, each head's logits, the distribution, the memory store, the
candidate set, the calibration map, the policy branch — each drawn once with
shape, dtype, byte size, and axis meanings; each transformation drawn as
before -> operation -> after with the fixture's exact values on the arrows.
Diagrams are generated from the same recorded values the tests assert on. Static
SVG under `assets/previews/` is the canonical committed form. Color is never the
only carrier of meaning; every diagram has a title, a description, and a numeric
table beside it.

**Every lesson measures three axes** and records them in its catalog entry:

| Axis | Required measurements | How |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | trainable parameters, active parameters per decision, feature-table bytes, packed-file bytes, memory-store bytes, trace bytes | `param_count`, explicit shape arithmetic, `file_size` |
| Speed | decisions per forward pass, encoder evaluations per turn, candidates scored per turn, and wall-clock microseconds per decision and milliseconds per training step | counted costs are the deterministic primary metric; `clock_ms()` is the machine-dependent secondary, reported with the binary version |
| Quality | per-head accuracy (action, topic, noul, score, recall), top-2 accuracy, per-category accuracy, NLL, Brier, ECE, reliability bins, coverage at target accuracy, teacher/student KL, abstention rate | the evaluation harness over the fixed split, with the rule engine as oracle |

**Accuracy alone is not a result.** Every quality claim reports the
accuracy-versus-coverage curve, because the number the application actually
needs is "at what threshold can code act autonomously, and how much of the
traffic does that cover":

| Threshold | Answered automatically | Accuracy when answered |
|---|---|---|
| 0.50 | ... | ... |
| 0.60 | ... | ... |
| 0.70 | ... | ... |
| 0.80 | ... | ... |
| 0.90 | ... | ... |

Every run appends one row to `docs/reference/results.md`, keyed by lesson ID,
configuration, and binary version, so the comparison matrix fills in as sagas
complete rather than being promised.

## Experimental progression

| Stage | Lesson | Mechanism | Question it answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | `EZ01` | classic ELIZA engine in MLPL (keywords, ranks, decomposition, reassembly) | the symbolic baseline and the labeling oracle |
| 0a | `EZ02` | the response table and deterministic transforms, isolated | what is the bounded output space, exactly? |
| 1 | `DS01` | rule + template corpus generator with curriculum categories | can we make labels cheaply and know what they teach? |
| 2 | `TD01` | fixed-class student: hashed features -> pool -> one action head | can a tiny model replace keyword rules at all? |
| 3 | `TD02` | factored multi-head: action, topic, 8 nouls, score — one pass | many typed decisions from one state representation |
| 4 | `TD03` | question-conditioned scorer `f(h_state, h_question, h_choice)` | can choices be *inputs*, so unseen candidates can be scored? |
| 5 | `CB01` | reliability, ECE, Brier, NLL; temperature / Platt / isotonic | does `.80` actually mean 80%? |
| 6 | `CB02` | calibration fine-tuning (`L_CE + lambda L_Brier`) | does training for calibration beat fixing it afterwards? |
| 7 | `AB01` | `OTHER` / `NONE` training and coverage curves | what does abstention buy, and at what threshold? |
| 8 | `MM01` | structured memory store and deterministic retrieval | state outside the model |
| 9 | `MM02` | the `RECALL` decision and the Decide -> Gather -> Decide loop | the model requests an operation; code performs it |
| 10 | `TS01` | independent scoring -> `grade_down` top-k -> comparative choice | the high-cardinality two-stage path |
| 11 | `TE01` | in-repo teacher exporting soft targets | a runnable teacher with no external dependency |
| 12 | `TE02` | external GPT teacher (gated), same fixture schema | linguistic diversity and indirection |
| 13 | `TE03` | teacher ensemble, disagreement as a signal | does consensus improve corpus quality? |
| 14 | `KD01` | soft-label distillation, `KL(teacher \|\| student)` vs `CE` | is the teacher's uncertainty worth keeping? |
| 15 | `AD01` | active distillation: student uncertainty selects what to label | how far does teacher cost fall? |
| 16 | `EN01` | encoder ladder: bag-of-words -> pool -> CNN -> GRU -> attention -> SSM | how much encoder does this decision surface need? |
| 17 | `MX01` | MoE encoder | is conditional compute worth it at this scale? |
| 18 | `RB01` | resource budget: INT8/INT4, packed file, microseconds per decision | what does the deployed artifact actually cost? |
| 19 | `MB01` | keyword-matcher yardstick, held-out-lexicon split | did the learned component actually buy anything? |

`MB01` is deliberately last in the table and first in spirit: `../moe-microscope`
recorded a docent that did not beat a deterministic matcher, and that honesty is
the standard here. Every learned lesson reports its margin over the matcher on
the same split, and a negative margin is published as a result.

## Visualization track, every saga

The instrument is dogfooded from Saga 1, not built at the end.

- Every lesson emits a `decision-trace-v1` document, pinned by hash under
  `fixtures/traces/`.
- Every saga ends with an instrument step: the new traces render in the Yew host
  with no lesson-specific Rust added, and any schema or budget gap is reported
  the way language findings are.
- Committed SVG diagrams remain the canonical README evidence; the instrument
  adds stepping and selection, never a second implementation of a lesson.
- The live (`mlpl-serve` SSE) path starts once three traces exist.

## Saga 1: foundation, probes, the ELIZA oracle, and the response table

1. **foundation-contract.** `agentrail setup`; `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
   `justfile`, `mlplunit.conf`, `scripts/`, `catalog/lessons.toml`, the docs
   skeleton, `COPYRIGHT`, `LICENSE`, and the README.
2. **language-probes.** The three Saga-1 probes above (`freeze`, two-argument
   scorer gradients, `experiment` inside a user function), each with a pinned
   mlplunit probe and a findings entry.
3. **eliza-engine (EZ01).** The classic engine in MLPL: keyword list with ranks,
   decomposition patterns, reassembly rules, the pronoun transform, and the
   memory stack ELIZA itself had. Tests pin its output on a fixed transcript so
   it is a *deterministic oracle*, not an approximation of one.
4. **response-table (EZ02).** The response table as committed data, with the
   byte-identity gate test and the diagram of the bounded output space.
5. **matcher-yardstick (MB01).** The keyword matcher scored on the evaluation
   split, with the held-out-lexicon split defined here so no later lesson can
   quietly choose an easier one.

Exit: a deterministic ELIZA runs, its output space is enumerated and gated, the
yardstick has a published number, and the probes have answers.

## Saga 2: the corpus and the first student

1. **corpus-generator (DS01).** Template and mutation generator producing all
   nine curriculum categories, with the oracle labeling everything it can. The
   split is fixed here and never regenerated.
2. **first-student (TD01).** Hashed word+bigram features (porting the technique
   from `../moe-microscope/lib/docent.mlpl`), mean pool, one action head,
   `cross_entropy`, `adam`. Parameter count printed in full.
3. **first-trace.** The `decision-trace-v1` schema, the first pinned trace, and
   the first instrument render.
4. **student-vs-matcher.** TD01 against MB01 on the same split, per category.

Exit: a learned selector exists, its margin over the matcher is published per
category, and one trace renders in the instrument.

## Saga 3: typed primitives and question-conditioned decisions

1. **factored-heads (TD02).** Action, topic, eight Nouls, and the score scale
   from one shared encoder in one forward pass. Per-head losses summed;
   binary cross-entropy composed for the Nouls. The "one pass, many decisions"
   diagram is drawn from real recorded values.
2. **decision-record.** The `choice` / `noul` / `score` MLPL contract, with the
   confidence and margin definitions fixed once and reused everywhere.
3. **question-conditioned-scorer (TD03).** `score_i = f(h_state, h_question,
   h_choice_i)`, trained over `(state, question, choices, answer)` tuples so the
   same model answers questions whose choices it never saw. Compared head to
   head with the fixed-head TD02 on the questions both can answer — the cost of
   generality, measured.
4. **cross-encoder-comparison.** The accurate-but-repeated cross-encoder against
   the shared-state encoder, on accuracy and on encoder evaluations per turn.

Exit: three primitives implemented, the general form works, and the generality
cost is a number.

## Saga 4: calibration and abstention

1. **calibration-measurement (CB01).** Reliability bins, ECE, Brier, NLL,
   and the reliability diagram composed from `scatter` + `line` + `baseline`.
2. **post-hoc-calibration.** Temperature scaling, Platt scaling, and isotonic
   regression (PAVA) from scratch, fitted on validation, compared on the same
   table: accuracy, ECE, Brier before and after.
3. **calibration-training (CB02).** `L = L_CE + lambda L_Brier`, swept over
   lambda, against the post-hoc baselines. The honest question this saga exists
   to answer: *at this scale, is anything beyond temperature scaling necessary?*
   A "no" is a publishable result.
4. **abstention (AB01).** `OTHER` / `NONE` with deliberate positives and hard
   negatives; the coverage-versus-accuracy table; the policy idiom
   `if confidence >= t { act } else { fallback }` shown in MLPL.
5. **instrument-calibration.** The instrument shows whether a distribution is
   raw or calibrated, and by what map.

Exit: the reliability diagram, the three-way calibration comparison, and the
coverage table are all in the results file and rendered in the instrument.

## Saga 5: conversation memory and two-stage selection

1. **memory-store (MM01).** The structured memory record, deterministic
   extraction, and the cheap retriever (keyword overlap, topic tag, recency)
   with its own accuracy number — retrieval quality measured separately from
   decision quality, because conflating them is how this gets misread.
2. **recall-decision (MM02).** The full Decide -> Gather -> Decide -> Act loop,
   with `NONE` in every candidate set and the `memory-negative` category
   carrying real weight.
3. **two-stage-selector (TS01).** Independent sigmoid scoring of up to 100
   memories, `grade_down` top-k, then a comparative softmax over the survivors;
   compared against single-stage selection over the same candidates on accuracy
   and on candidates scored per turn. This is the mechanism TypeSafe describes
   for high-cardinality choices, and we arrived at it independently for this
   problem — worth saying plainly in the write-up.
4. **memory-instrument.** The instrument's memory pane: store, retrieved
   candidates, the second decision, and the `NONE` threshold.

Exit: "Earlier you said..." works without a context window, and the cost of
conversation length is measured rather than assumed.

## Saga 6: teachers, distillation, and active labeling

1. **in-repo-teacher (TE01).** The larger MLPL TDM and its soft-target fixture
   schema.
2. **external-teacher (TE02).** The gated local-model path, same schema,
   recorded identity/revision/budget, documented skip status when unavailable.
3. **teacher-ensemble (TE03).** Three teachers, agreement as a weight,
   disagreement routed to the hard set. Dataset quality measured as downstream
   student accuracy, not as a self-reported score.
4. **distillation (KD01).** `KL(teacher || student)` against plain `CE`, and the
   mixed objective, with the label-authority hierarchy enforced in code so the
   rule engine always outranks a teacher.
5. **active-distillation (AD01).** Cheap student triage: confident examples skip
   the teacher, uncertain ones are labeled. Report teacher calls saved at equal
   student accuracy — the number that makes this worth doing.

Exit: the distillation pipeline runs end to end offline, and teacher cost per
point of student accuracy is a published curve.

## Saga 7: the encoder frontier and the deployed artifact

1. **encoder-ladder (EN01).** Bag-of-words logistic regression, mean pool, MLP,
   CNN, GRU, 1-head attention, and a state-space block — same corpus, same
   heads, same split. Plotted as accuracy and ECE against parameters and
   microseconds per decision, so the knee of the curve is visible.
2. **moe-encoder (MX01).** A routed encoder, connecting directly to
   `../moe-microscope`'s conditional-compute work.
3. **resource-budget (RB01).** INT8 then INT4 weights, the packed file, bytes
   and microseconds per decision, and the quality lost at each step.
4. **pocket-therapist.** The deployed artifact: the packed file plus the response
   table, running the whole loop with no generative model present.

Exit: the smallest configuration that meets a stated accuracy-and-calibration
bar is identified by measurement, and it ships as a file.

## Saga 8: the instrument, complete

1. **instrument-complete.** Every decision kind, stepping, selection, threshold
   overlays, the policy trace, and the side-by-side classic/learned comparison
   mode in one page.
2. **ambiguity-theatre.** The deliberately ambiguous inputs — `I dreamed my
   mother was a computer.` — with the policy panel editable, so a viewer can
   watch `if confidence < .50 -> DEFAULT` and `if dream > .30 -> DREAM` produce
   different behavior from *identical* model output. Prediction and policy,
   visibly separated.
3. **live-path.** The `mlpl-serve` SSE path: edit the lesson, rerun, watch the
   trace stream.
4. **second-slide.** A campus-navigation trace rendered by the same instrument
   with no new Rust, proving the abstraction.

Exit: the instrument plays every pinned trace, the ambiguity demonstration
works, and a non-ELIZA trace renders unmodified.

## Saga 9: findings and recommendations

The report: what a tiny typed decision model can and cannot do; where
calibration training paid and where temperature scaling was enough; what the
learned selector bought over keyword matching, per category, with the
held-out-lexicon result stated plainly; the teacher-cost curve; the parameter /
latency / accuracy / ECE frontier; and an explicit list of what we could *not*
determine about Jev from public information, so the boundary between our
measurements and their claims stays legible.

## Cross-cutting gates

- Every executable behavior starts with native mlplunit coverage; `just check`
  is the full pre-commit gate and grows with each lesson's demo and fixture
  freshness checks.
- Every `.mlpl` file has a module-purpose comment, every user function has a
  first-expression docstring, and canonical formatting is checked before commit
  and push with `scripts/check-mlpl-style`.
- **The no-generation gate.** A test asserts that every string Jeviza can emit
  is byte-identical to a committed response-table entry, reached by index. This
  runs on every commit. It is the repository's central claim, so it is enforced
  mechanically.
- Every lesson satisfies the visual and measurement contract and adds a catalog
  entry naming its source, tests, previews, trace, fixture, triple, and
  implementation form.
- Every quality claim carries its per-category breakdown, its calibration
  numbers, and its margin over the `MB01` matcher on the same split.
- Every language or host gap gets a reproducer under `probes/`, a pinned
  mlplunit probe, a workaround, and a findings entry, in the same step it is met.
- Lessons are deterministic, bounded, standalone, and honest about which work
  runs in MLPL, in a builtin, in Rust, or in a simulator.
- Sibling repositories remain read-only; their work is written as a handoff.
- `sw-checklist` applies to the Rust crates.

## Non-goals

- A better chatbot. Response quality is fixed by a 1966 table and is not an
  objective; only *selection* quality is measured.
- Any generative path at inference. No decoder, no sampling into text, no
  string the response table does not contain.
- Reproducing Jev, its architecture, or RLCD. We reproduce the published
  *behavioral contract* and the *objective*, and say so every time.
- Claiming schema conformance implies correctness. A typed output cannot be
  outside the permitted space; it can still be the wrong choice, and the
  coverage tables exist to say how often.
- Treating a teacher's stated confidence as a calibrated probability.
- ELIZA-specific types in the Rust instrument crates.
- Training on a microcontroller; the MCU/NPU/FPGA track is an inference target
  and is out of scope until after Saga 7.
- Modifying any sibling repository from a saga in this repository.
